definition: Energy markets should generally be assumed illiquid rather than liquid — it can be difficult to find a counterparty or to convert a position back into cash.
core_idea: Illiquidity in energy markets stems from heavy reliance on privately negotiated bilateral contracts, the narrowing of liquidity in exchange-traded contracts beyond the near term, the location- and time-specific nature of physical delivery, and a tendency for market participants to move in the same direction at the same time, leaving few counterparties on the other side.
key_points: Directly negotiated (bilateral/OTC) contracts are common in energy and are inherently harder to exit than exchange-traded ones.
Even liquid exchange-traded contracts (e.g., NYMEX WTI Crude Oil) concentrate most volume in the first few delivery months, with open interest dropping off quickly further out.

Delivery is tied to specific times and locations; a facility in an unusual location (author's example: Alaska) may have very few counterparties able to physically deliver power there, and no nearby exchange-traded contract to reference.

A bespoke bilateral deal can be nearly impossible to unwind: other market participants may be suspicious of why the original counterparty wants out of a trade that looked good enough to enter, and the original physical counterparty (e.g., the industrial facility) may have no incentive to unwind a deal that locked in favorable prices for them.

Energy market participants (e.g., refiners, power plant owners) tend to converge on the same market view at the same time, which undermines liquidity since a liquid market needs both willing buyers and willing sellers, ideally in balance.
trading_implications: Positions taken via bilateral/OTC deals or in longer-dated/off-standard-location energy contracts should be assumed hard to exit, not just hard to price.
Herding behavior among energy market participants can dry up liquidity precisely when a trader most wants to adjust a position.
caveats: Assuming that because a contract is exchange-traded, it will remain liquid at all maturities.
Assuming a profitable bilateral trade can easily be exited if desired.
